top_strength: Calvin's pricing block is genuinely good and it is the reason this call converted to a warm 'perfect.' He opened it the right way - 'Well, yeah, our pricing is really simple' - and then actually delivered on simple: rate, what triggers the clock, what is included, and what is not, in one clean pass. 'it would be a 220 hourly rate and that would take effect once they actually got on site' is exactly the on-site trigger the rubric wants, and he followed it with 'we do a two and a half hour minimum. Once we exceed the minimum we bill in fifteen minute increments until the move is completed so you just pay for the time use.' His budget framing was better still - he priced the packing supplies down rather than up, unprompted: typical is 'about $189 and packing supplies for a one bedroom apartment pack but it's gonna be quite a bit less than that for, for this cause there's no close it's probably gonna be more along the lines of like maybe $50 or $60,' and closed the loop with 'You only pay for the supplies we actually use.' He also volunteered the friction-removers proactively when she raised a possible date change: 'there's no fee to reschedule. There's no deposit to book and there's no cancellation fees either' - and he caught the weekday tier without being asked, 'on the thirtieth it would be the hourly rate is only $208. Our weekday pricing is a little lower than Fridays and Saturdays.' He read the situation too, offering 'I can email this all to you if you want as well. So you don't have to take notes' to a customer who was driving, then closing with 'I know you left the office. So I'll let you go now.'
coaching_note: One line was missing and it was worth the whole call: the no-risk hold. Katie told him she is the office manager and that approval sits with her head of facilities - 'she'll give me the thumbs up and then we can keep moving' - so a same-call close was genuinely blocked, but a date hold was not. He had already confirmed 'We do have availability on the twenty fifth' and later 'we would have availability on the thirtieth as well,' and he knew there was no deposit and no cancellation fee. He should have said it while she was still on the line: 'Since there's no deposit and no cancellation fee, let me pencil you in on the twenty fifth right now so it's protected while your facilities lead signs off - if it moves to the thirtieth I'll just slide it, no charge.' Instead the no-deposit fact surfaced ten lines later as a reactive answer and the call ended with a lead sitting in an email queue on a corporate move with a hard lease deadline. Second, he left the Save Your Ass speech on the table after the customer teed it up herself: 'we'll be there we can clear things out before you guys make it.' That is an open invitation for 'great - anything you can consolidate or take in a carload before we get there comes straight off the clock,' and on a job he quoted at four to five hours it is real money to her and real efficiency to the crew. Third, for estimate accuracy: he built the whole quote on a one-bedroom without ever asking what floor she is on, whether there is an elevator, or how far the walk to the truck is - and he assumed the second bedroom would be cleared ('it was a one bedroom apartment') on a move that might land on the twenty fifth, the same day staff are supposed to grab that furniture. If it runs on the twenty fifth with the second bedroom still full and a third-floor walkup, the $880-$1,100 range is wrong before the crew arrives.
phone_presence_notes: Pleasant, easy and well-paced, with a nice piece of situational awareness at the end ('I know you left the office. So I'll let you go now'), but the warmth is procedural - her name is used once and never again, acknowledgments are 'Okay' and 'Gotcha,' and the core of the call is one long uninterrupted pricing block.
audio_review_reason: The pricing and clock explanation runs as a single unbroken turn with four separate customer interjections ('Got it,' 'Okay,' 'Got it,' 'Okay') stacked against it, which the transcript cannot resolve into either an engaged back-and-forth or a rep talking straight through his customer's check-ins. That distinction is the difference between a 3 and a 2 here, and it also determines whether the coaching is 'add the differentiators' or 'slow down and leave gaps.'
